title: CASE OF CHAPMAN v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
conclusion: No violation of Art. 8;No violation of P1-1;No violation of Art. 6-1;No violation of Art. 14
summary:
In Chapman v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Ms. Jane Chapman, identified as a Gypsy by birth—a term encompassed within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers—brought a case against the United Kingdom. The heart of the case lay in the persistent vulnerability faced by Roma and Traveller families who, due to a lack of authorised sites, are forced into a cycle of eviction, instability, and disrupted access to education and healthcare. Ms. Chapman and her family, lifelong travellers in Hertfordshire, purchased land in 1985 to settle in a mobile home after years of being moved on by authorities and facing harassment detrimental to their children’s education and family health. Despite applying for planning permission to live on their own land, the local council repeatedly refused, citing Green Belt restrictions, and issued enforcement notices. The family faced fines and, after exhausting appeals, were compelled to return to a nomadic life, again suffering instability and educational disruption for their children.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), 6 (right to a fair hearing), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Court found no violation of these rights, concluding that the planning controls pursued a legitimate aim and that sufficient consideration had been given to Ms. Chapman’s circumstances. While no remedies were awarded, the case is significant as it highlights the ongoing challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in securing stable accommodation in Europe. Set against a backdrop of historical marginalisation and legislative changes in the UK, Chapman v. the United Kingdom remains a landmark in the struggle for equal treatment and recognition of the rights of Roma and Travellers.
